t.4.1.1: Having gone to that lotus lake, crowded with lotuses, water lilies and fish, Rāma, accompanied by Saumitri, lamented, his senses agitated.
t.4.1.3: O Saumitri, behold the forest of Pampā, lovely to look upon, where trees shine like mountains, as if crowned with peaks.
t.4.1.2: The moment he beheld it, his senses trembled with joy; and, falling under the sway of longing, he spoke these words to Saumitri.
t.4.1.4: But as for me, scorched by grief, anxieties truly torment me, through the sorrow of Bharata and through the abduction of Vaidehī.
t.4.1.5: This grassy meadow, blue and yellow, shines forth all the more, strewn with the many kinds of flowers from the trees as though spread with coverlets.
t.4.1.6: O Saumitri, this season, with its pleasant breezes, is full of love's longing; this fragrant month of spring is rich in scents, and its trees have burst into flower and fruit.
t.4.1.7: Behold, Saumitri, the beauty of the forests rich in blossoms, as they shed showers of flowers like rain-clouds pouring down their rain.
t.4.1.8: And on the lovely rocky plateaus, the many kinds of forest trees, set swaying by the force of the wind, strew the earth with their blossoms.
t.4.1.9: The breeze, cool as sandalwood, blows pleasant to the touch through the honey-scented woods, accompanied by the humming of bees.
t.4.1.10: On the lovely mountain plateaus, the mountains, their peaks thick with great flowering and charming trees, shine forth in splendor.
t.4.1.11: And see these karṇikāra trees all around, their tips in full bloom, covered as if with gold, like men clad in yellow garments.
t.4.1.12: O Saumitri, this spring, resounding with the calls of many kinds of birds, inflames the grief of me who am separated from Sītā.
t.4.1.13: For Manmatha torments me, overwhelmed as I am by grief, and the joyful cuckoo, calling out loudly, challenges me.
t.4.1.14: O Lakṣmaṇa, this joyful gallinule, crying out loudly by the lovely forest waterfall, will make me grieve, possessed as I am by love.
t.4.1.15: O Saumitri, the sweet-voiced birds, mingling with their mates, rejoice in their own flocks and are gladdened by the bhṛṅgarāja birds.
t.4.1.16: For that fawn-eyed lady torments me, O Saumitri, overpowered as I am by anxiety and grief, and so does the cruel wind of the forest in the month of Caitra.
t.4.1.17: On the slopes of the mountains, the peacocks, surrounded by their peahens, inflame the love in me, who am already overcome by love.
t.4.1.18: Look, Lakṣmaṇa! On the mountain slopes this peahen, tormented by Manmatha, dances close beside her mate, the peacock, as he dances.
t.4.1.19: Surely the beloved of the peacock in the forest has not been carried off by a rākṣasa; but for me this dwelling without my beloved in the month of flowers is exceedingly hard to bear.
t.4.1.21: Delighted birds in flocks utter their sweet, soft cries, as though calling to one another, and they stir in me the madness of longing.
t.4.1.20: See, Lakṣmaṇa, the flowers of the forests, so richly laden with their burden of blossoms at winter's end: for me they bear no fruit.
t.4.1.22: Surely Sītā, fallen under another's power, grieves just as I do, she, my beloved, dark-hued, lotus-petal-eyed and gentle of speech.
t.4.1.23: This wind, bearing the scent of flowers, pleasant to the touch and bringing coolness, feels like fire to me as I keep thinking of my beloved.
t.4.1.25: This bird there is surely the doorkeeper of Vaidehī; this winged one will lead me into the presence of the large-eyed lady.
t.4.1.24: Now, while I am without her, that winged bird, the crow, perched upon a tree, has burst into cries and caws out joyfully.
t.4.1.26: Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, the clamor in the forest, heightening passion, of the birds warbling in the trees whose tops are in flower.
t.4.1.27: Look, Saumitri, amid the colorful rows of trees of Pampā, the lotuses shine in the water like the young rising sun.
t.4.1.28: Here is Pampā, her waters clear and tranquil, spread wide with lotuses and blue water-lilies, thronged with haṃsas and kāraṇḍava ducks, and filled with fragrant saugandhika flowers.
t.4.1.29: Ever accompanied by cakravāka birds, with lovely tablelands and woodland stretches around it, the lake shines with herds of elephants and deer that come seeking water.
t.4.1.30: For my sight longs to gaze upon the petals of the lotus buds, O Lakṣmaṇa, thinking that they resemble the two eyes of Sītā.
t.4.1.31: Mingled with the filaments of lotuses and issuing forth from between the trees, the enchanting breeze blows like the breath of Sītā.
t.4.1.32: O Saumitri, look: on the southern slope of the mountain by Pampā stands a flowering karṇikāra, its slender trunk supremely beautiful.
t.4.1.33: This king of mountains, adorned with minerals, abundantly sends forth many-coloured dust, stirred up by the force of the wind.
t.4.1.34: And the mountain slopes, O Saumitri, look as if they were ablaze, set alight on every side by the kiṃśuka trees, leafless yet lovely all around and covered everywhere in full blossom.
t.4.1.35: And these clusters of mālatī and mallikā growing on the banks of the Pampā, closely intertwined and fragrant with honey, and the karavīra trees too, are in full bloom.
t.4.1.36: Ketakīs, sinduvāras and vāsantīs are in full bloom, and everywhere there are fragrant mādhavīs and clusters of kunda bushes.
t.4.1.37: The ciribilvas and madhūkas, the vañjulas and bakulas, the campakas and tilakas, and the nāgavṛkṣas too are in full bloom.
t.4.1.38: Nīpas and varaṇas too, and date palms in full bloom, aṅkolas and kuraṇṭas, cūrṇakas and pāribhadrakas.
t.4.1.39: Mango trees and pāṭali trees, and kovidāras in full blossom, as well as mucukundas and arjunas, are seen on the slopes of the mountains.
t.4.1.41: O Saumitri, on the mountain slopes, carpets of many kinds, glowing yellow and red, have been spread by those very flowers of various kinds scattered there.
t.4.1.40: Ketakas and uddālakas, śirīṣas, śiṃśapās and dhavas, śālmalīs and kiṃśukas, red kurabakas as well, tiniśas and naktamālas, sandalwood trees and syandanas too are here.
t.4.1.42: Look, Saumitri, at the blossoming of the trees at winter's end, for in this month of flowers the trees have burst into bloom as if in rivalry with one another.
t.4.1.43: And look, O Saumitri, at this lake of cool waters, filled with lotuses, where cakravāka birds wander and kāraṇḍava ducks dwell.
t.4.1.44: Behold Pampā, filled with plava birds and krauñcas and frequented by boars and deer; she shines all the more with the birds warbling all around.
t.4.1.45: As I remember my beloved, the dusky, moon-faced one with eyes like lotuses, the many kinds of joyful birds seem to kindle my longing.
t.4.1.46: Look at the stags on the bright-hued mountain ridges, accompanied by their does, while I, by contrast, have been parted from Vaidehī, whose eyes are like a fawn's.
t.4.1.47: Lamenting thus there, his mind stricken by grief, he gazed upon the auspicious Pampā, lovely and bearing delightful waters.
t.4.1.48: Swiftly surveying the whole forest with its waterfalls and caves, the great-souled one, his mind agitated and stricken with grief, reflected and then set out together with Lakṣmaṇa.
t.4.1.49: Together the two of them set out for that Ṛṣyamūka, frequented by Sugrīva and his monkeys. But on seeing those two of great might, Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, the monkeys became frightened.
